title: Session slice checkpointing and revival spec
author: Asha Patel
content:
Overview

This document specifies the design, operational patterns, and validation playbooks for session slice checkpointing and revival in the Redwood serving runtime. The goal is to enable long-lived conversational/stateful sessions to survive eviction, migration, and kernel-level preemption while minimizing memory and latency overhead. The spec covers data formats, storage contracts, scheduler interactions, profiling signals to monitor, benchmark tests to prove cost/latency trade-offs, and a runnable incident playbook for recovery.

Goals
- Minimize user-visible latency when reviving an evicted session (target: 95th percentile revival < 120 ms on dedicated pools).
- Bound extra memory cost per active-sliced session to <= 5% of total stream memory on average workloads.
- Ensure safety: revived sessions must restore deterministic KV-cache and decoder prefix state for fidelity-sensitive workloads (evaluations/QA).
- Make slice checkpoints resumable across kernel variants and quantization profiles.

Glossary and components
- Session: logical conversation or stateful sequence from the Redwood API.
- Slice: a contiguous window of model execution state (kv-cache entries + decoder prefix metadata) small enough to checkpoint and transfer. Typical slice = latest N tokens' kv-deltas where N is configured per model.
- Checkpoint: serialized slice persisted to backing storage (in-memory cache + tiered durable store).
- Revival Agent: runtime component that reconstructs session state from checkpoints and orchestrates warmstart requests to the kernel-dispatcher.
- Slice-Manager: component responsible for creating, pruning, and expiring slices according to policy.
- Kernel-Dispatcher: the serving runtime component that maps requests to GPU kernels and manages scheduling/eviction.

Design overview
1) Slice boundaries and frequency
- Default slice length: 256 tokens for decoder-first models, 128 tokens for decoder-only smaller models.
- Create rolling checkpoints after either: 256 tokens since last slice OR 10 seconds since last activity, whichever comes first. This balances write amplification and revival granularity.
- The Slice-Manager supports adaptive slicing: for high-entropy sessions (many new tokens / variable seq lengths) the slice size may shrink to 128 to reduce revival cost.

2) Checkpoint format (JSON + binary KV blob)
- Checkpoint envelope (JSON, small): {\n    "version": "v1",\n    "session_id": "<uuid>",\n    "slice_index": "<int>",\n    "model": "<model-id>",\n    "seq_range": [<start>,<end>],\n    "created_at": "<iso>",\n    "kernel_hint": "<kernel-config>",\n    "affinity_hint": "<hw-pool>"\n  }
- Binary blob: optimized, compressed KV-delta + small decoder-state table. Blob layout includes a small CRC32 and LZ4 compression. The revival path validates CRC before load.

3) Storage tiers and consistency
- Ephemeral tier (fast): memory-backed LRU cache co-located with the slice's active host (store name: session-slice-cache). TTL default: 5 minutes.
- Durable tier (cold): a regional object store (store name: session-checkpoints), retention default: 30 days for dedicated customers, 7 days for hosted default.
- Write policy: write-through to ephemeral tier synchronously, enqueue background upload to durable tier. On background upload failures the Slice-Manager retries with exponential backoff; failures are surfaced to metrics.

4) Eviction and revival policy
- Eviction triggers: memory pressure signals, kernel preemption, node decommission, scaling down. When eviction is decided, the slice is pinned and the Slice-Manager emits a checkpoint creation event.
- Revival flow: client request hits routing layer -> routing checks session metadata -> if session not resident, routing invokes Revival Agent -> Revival Agent fetches checkpoint from ephemeral tier (fallback to durable) -> validates and streams KV-deltas to kernel-dispatcher using the warmstart API -> kernel acknowledges reconstructed prefix -> request proceeds.
- Fallback semantics: if checkpoint not found or corrupted, the Revival Agent constructs a degraded session with best-effort prefix (last N tokens in user-visible transcript) and annotates the response with a telemetry flag trace.revival.degraded=true.

Kernel scheduling interactions
- Warmstart handshake: kernel-dispatcher exposes warmstart endpoints that accept a slice_id, kernel_hint, and resume token. Warmstart operations are prioritized into a separate scheduling lane with admission limits to avoid blocking new short-lived requests.
- Preemption coordination: Schedulers must not preempt an in-flight warmstart unless safe-checks pass. Safe-checks include ensuring the revived KV-cache has been persisted to ephemeral tier and that no concurrent write is ongoing.
- Admission controls and credits: revival lanes consume kernel-credit units at a 2x weight vs steady inference tokens for the first 50ms to reflect the higher GPU work to reconstruct KV-cache. This weight decays after successful warmstart.

Profiling and observability playbook
- Signals to capture for each slice lifecycle: slice.create.latency, slice.upload.duration, slice.fetch.latency(ephemeral), slice.fetch.latency(durable), slice.validation.failures, revival.handshake.latency, revival.fidelity-flag, revival.memory-overhead.
- Trace correlation: include tags session_id, slice_index, kernel_id, request_id to enable end-to-end reconstruction of a revival path in a single APM span.
- Sampling policy: sample 100% of failed revivals and 1% of successful revivals. For high-SLA customers sample 5% of successful revivals.
- Profiling recipe (step-by-step):
  1. Reproduce a node eviction in the staging cluster with a mix of slice sizes.
  2. Collect full traces for the affected session_ids and kernel dispatch logs.
  3. Measure revival.handshake.latency distribution and correlate with kernel_hint and slice size.
  4. Verify CRC and decompression time dominates or not. If CRC >> 20ms, investigate I/O or CPU noise.

Benchmarking suite and acceptance criteria
- Bench types: micro (single-slice create/fetch), integration (eviction + revival under steady traffic), stress (mass eviction under bursty traffic), fidelity (regression tests against ground-truth conversation transcripts).
- Sample test: Revival whole-path SLO test\  - Setup: 1k concurrent sessions, each with 3 slices in ephemeral tier; trigger rolling eviction of 20% nodes; replay 1k requests that require revival.\  - Success criteria: 95th percentile end-to-end revival latency < 120 ms, revival failure rate < 0.2%, and post-revival model output match baseline (BLEU-like metric for structured responses > 0.98).
- Cost benchmark: measure extra tokens and kernel time used during revival and report per-10k-revivals cost delta. Target operator-visible CPU overhead < 7% of baseline during typical workloads.

Release, rollout, and compatibility notes
- Versioning: checkpoint envelope includes version field. v1 -> v2 migration requires in-place upgrade of Slice-Manager and Revival Agent. We support backward-reading: Revival Agent v2 can read v1 envelopes; Kernel warmstart must negotiate kernel_hint.
- Feature flagging: rollout under feature flag runtime.slice-checkpointing.enabled = false by default. Canary pool (5% traffic) -> 25% -> 100% with observability gates (revival latency & failure thresholds).
- Model compatibility: ensure that quantized or sharded kernels expose a compatible warmstart shim; otherwise Runtime will fallback to degraded revival. Document model whitelist for full-fidelity revival.

Operational runbook (incident-oriented)
- Symptom A: revival failure rate spike (>0.5% over 5m)\  1. Check slice.upload.duration and ephemeral cache saturation metrics.\  2. If ephemeral cache OOMs: increase TTL on session-slice-cache or scale slice-cache nodes; call on-call storage lead.\  3. If durable store upload errors: inspect uploader logs, check object-store rate limits and retry queue size.\  4. If CRC failures: inspect slice-manager CPU load, investigate kernel library version mismatch.\  5. Mitigation: temporarily set runtime.slice-checkpointing.enabled=false for the affected pool and trigger live-migration of pinned sessions using migration script: scripts/migrate-pinned-sessions --graceful
- Symptom B: long revival handshake latency (95p > 250 ms)\  1. Correlate with kernel_hint and kernel-dispatcher saturations.\  2. If warmstart lane starved: adjust admission control to add +1 revival-worker for 10 minutes.\  3. If decompression dominates: offload decompression to dedicated CPU pool or increase ephemeral tier locality.\  4. Mitigation: set a temporary admission cap and route new sessions to a lower-latency fallback model.
- Emergency recovery (checkpoint corruption widespread)\  1. Flip a global flag to force degraded revivals and annotate requests (trace.revival.degraded=true).\  2. Run a recovery job to rehydrate session state from transcript replay for critical customers.\  3. Post-incident: run forensic profiling, bump checkpoint CRC verification and add checksum telemetry.

Known issues and constraints
- Cross-kernel warmstart divergence: certain experimental kernels change internal kv-serialization layout causing revival CRC mismatch. Workaround: add kernel_hint mapping table in the envelope and pin those sessions to compatible kernels.
- High write amplification for very chatty sessions: customers with avg token rate > 50 tokens/sec will cause many slice writes; recommend configuring adaptive slice policy or applying per-session write-rate throttle.
- Replay determinism: revival assumes deterministic KV replay; non-deterministic model ops (custom kernels with randomized ops) may yield fidelity drift. Such kernels must be added to the non-revivable list in runtime config.

Ownership, telemetry, and next steps
- Owner: runtime-session-team (primary), kernel-team (warmstart contract), infra-storage (checkpoint storage).
- Dashboards to create: Revival health (failure rate, latency P50/P95/P99), Slice storage cost by customer, Revival fidelity regressions by model.
- Next work items:
  - v2 checkpoint with signed manifests for better integrity checks.
  - Chunked streaming revival to reduce worst-case tail (prototype Q2 2026).
  - Operator controls for per-customer slice retention policies.

References and related docs
- See: runtime-feature-lifecycle-and-sunset-playbook-2026 (migration guidance), cold-start-warmup-strategies-and-entropy-reduction-2025 (warmstart heuristics), kernel-admission-matrix-and-signal-negotiation-manual-2026 (scheduler contract).

Appendix: sample checkpoint envelope (human-readable)
{\n  "version": "v1",\n  "session_id": "6a9f8c1a-...",\n  "slice_index": "42",\n  "model": "rw-instruct-13b-v2",\n  "seq_range": [10240,10496],\n  "created_at": "2026-02-28T11:45:30Z",\n  "kernel_hint": "tiled-sharded-v3",\n  "affinity_hint": "pool-us-west-2a"\n}

(End of document)
